name: King's Gambit Accepted
summary: In the King's Gambit Accepted (1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3) Black grabs the f4-pawn while White develops rapidly for a kingside attack.
intro: The King's Gambit Accepted arises after 1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3. Black takes the offered pawn and White immediately develops the knight to f3, ruling out the annoying ...Qh4+ and preparing to reclaim the initiative. It is the archetypal Romantic-era opening, in which White trades a pawn for open lines, a lead in development, and a lasting attack against Black's king.

sections.heading: Strategic ideas
paragraphs: By playing 2.f4 White offers the f-pawn to deflect Black's e5-pawn and seize the centre with a later d4. Once Black accepts with 2...exf4, the move 3.Nf3 serves two purposes: it develops a piece toward the kingside and pre-empts the check on h4 that would otherwise disrupt White's castling. In return for the pawn White obtains a half-open f-file, rapid piece deployment, and the prospect of a broad pawn centre, while Black must either cling to the extra material on f4 or return it to complete development safely.

The central imbalance defines the struggle. White typically follows with d4, Bxf4 or Bc4, and short castling, after which the rook on f1 bears down the f-file toward f7, the softest point in Black's camp. Black's task is to neutralise White's initiative and convert the extra pawn into a lasting endgame edge; if Black can trade queens and blunt the attack, the material tells. The recurring tension is therefore development and king safety for White against material and consolidation for Black.

sections.heading: Main variations
paragraphs: The classical continuation is 3...g5, in which Black grimly defends the f4-pawn with the pawn chain. This is the gateway to the sharpest lines: 4.h4 g4 leads to the Kieseritzky Gambit (5.Ne5) and the Allgaier Gambit (5.Ng5), while 4.Bc4 introduces the Muzio complex where White may sacrifice the f3-knight for a raging attack. These variations produce some of the most forcing and heavily analysed positions in all of opening theory.

Modern practice often steers Black away from ...g5. The Modern Defence 3...d5 returns the pawn at once to open lines for development and free the light-squared bishop. Fischer's recommendation 3...d6, the so-called Fischer Defence, prepares ...g5 under improved circumstances by covering e5 and giving the king's bishop a retreat. Other solid tries include 3...Be7, aiming for ...Bh4+ ideas, and 3...Nf6, striking at e4 and developing naturally rather than grabbing space on the kingside.

sections.heading: History and background
paragraphs: The King's Gambit is among the oldest recorded openings, discussed in the sixteenth-century treatises of Ruy López and Polerio and dominating elite play throughout the Romantic era of the nineteenth century. Masters such as Anderssen, Morphy, and later Spielmann and Bronstein wielded it as a vehicle for spectacular attacking chess. Improvements in defensive technique gradually reduced its standing at the highest level, and today it is regarded as a bold surprise weapon rather than a main-line try, though Bobby Fischer's famous article proposing 3...d6 kept its theory alive. It remains beloved by attacking players and club competitors for the rich, double-edged positions it produces.

keyIdeas: 2.f4 offers a pawn to deflect ...e5 and prepare a broad centre with d4.
3.Nf3 develops with tempo and prevents the disruptive ...Qh4+.
White's compensation is a lead in development, open lines, and the half-open f-file.
The f7-square is the target of White's attack once the f-file opens.
Black aims to hold or return the pawn, complete development, and reach a safe endgame.
Modern defences ...d5 and Fischer's ...d6 avoid the wildest ...g5 lines.

white: Play d4 to build a strong pawn centre and open lines for the pieces.
Recapture on f4 with the bishop and castle short to activate the f1-rook.
Develop the bishop to c4 to eye f7 and support a kingside assault.
In the ...g5 lines, strike with h4 to break up Black's kingside pawn chain.
Use the half-open f-file and rapid development to attack before Black consolidates.
black: Hold the extra pawn with ...g5 and accept sharp, forcing complications.
Return the pawn with the Modern Defence ...d5 to free development and equalise.
Play Fischer's ...d6 to prepare ...g5 safely and give the bishop a retreat.
Complete development quickly and aim to trade queens to blunt White's attack.
Convert the extra pawn in a simplified position once the initiative is neutralised.
